questions.question: What type of relation is $R=\{(a,b),(b,c),(b,a),(c,b)\}$ on the set $A=\{a,b,c\}$?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Symmetric

**Check reflexivity:** a relation on $A$ is reflexive if $(x,x)\in R$ for every $x\in A$. Here none of $(a,a)$, $(b,b)$, $(c,c)$ belongs to $R$, so $R$ is **not** reflexive.

**Check symmetry:** for every $(x,y)\in R$ we need $(y,x)\in R$:
- $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,a)\in R$ ✓
- $(b,c)\in R$ and $(c,b)\in R$ ✓
- $(b,a)\in R$ and $(a,b)\in R$ ✓
- $(c,b)\in R$ and $(b,c)\in R$ ✓

Every pair comes with its reverse, so $R$ **is symmetric**.

**Check transitivity:** $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,c)\in R$ force $(a,c)\in R$ — but $(a,c)\notin R$. So $R$ is **not** transitive.

$$\therefore\ R\ \text{is symmetric only}$$

(It is exactly the relation 'differs from' on a three-letter set, which is the standard example of a symmetric-but-neither-reflexive-nor-transitive relation.)

questions.question: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is such that $f(x)=5x+4$, then $f^{-1}(x)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{x-4}{5}$

**Step 1 — put $y=f(x)$ and solve for $x$:**
$$y=5x+4$$
$$5x=y-4$$
$$x=\frac{y-4}{5}$$

**Step 2 — interchange the names** ($y$ becomes the new input):
$$f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x-4}{5}$$

**Check both compositions:**
$$f\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=5\cdot\frac{x-4}{5}+4=x-4+4=x\ ✓$$
$$f^{-1}\left(f(x)\right)=\frac{(5x+4)-4}{5}=\frac{5x}{5}=x\ ✓$$

Since $f$ is a linear function with non-zero slope it is one-one and onto $\mathbb{R}$, so the inverse is defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: For any operation $*$ defined on $\mathbb{Q}$ as $a*b=\dfrac{a+b}{3}$, then $1*2=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $1$

Substitute $a=1$, $b=2$ in the definition $a*b=\dfrac{a+b}{3}$:
$$1*2=\frac{1+2}{3}=\frac33=1$$

$$\therefore\ 1*2=1$$

**Observation about the operation:** it is commutative, since $a+b=b+a$. It is *not* associative: $(1*2)*3=1*3=\dfrac43$, while $1*(2*3)=1*\dfrac53=\dfrac{1+5/3}{3}=\dfrac89$ — the two differ, so $(\mathbb{Q},*)$ is not a group. This topic belongs to the deleted portion of the syllabus but the computation itself is trivial.

questions.question: Principal value of $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ is
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

The principal branch of $\sin^{-1}$ is $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. We need the angle in that interval whose sine is $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$$\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\qquad \frac{\pi}{3}\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\ ✓$$

$$\therefore\ \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=\frac{\pi}{3}=60^{\circ}$$

**Why not $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$?** Although $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ as well, $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ lies outside the principal range, so it is not the principal value.

questions.question: $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $2\tan^{-1}x$

**Step 1 — substitute $x=\tan\theta$**, i.e. $\theta=\tan^{-1}x$ with $\theta\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$:
$$\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}=\frac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}$$

**Step 2 — use $\dfrac{1-\tan^{2}\theta}{1+\tan^{2}\theta}=\cos2\theta$** (divide numerator and denominator of $\cos2\theta=\dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta-\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta}$ by $\cos^{2}\theta$):
$$\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}=\cos2\theta$$

**Step 3 — take the inverse cosine:**
$$\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\right)=\cos^{-1}\left(\cos2\theta\right)=2\theta=2\tan^{-1}x$$

provided $2\theta\in[0,\pi]$, which holds for $x\ge0$; for $x<0$ the expression equals $-2\tan^{-1}x$ in the standard branch, so the printed identity is understood for $x\ge0$.

$$\therefore\ \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}\right)=2\tan^{-1}x$$

**Numerical check:** at $x=1$ the left side is $\cos^{-1}0=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and the right side $2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ ✓; at $x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ the left side is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1-\frac13}{1+\frac13}=\cos^{-1}\dfrac12=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and the right side $2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ ✓.

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 3&6\end{bmatrix}$, then $3A=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\ 9&18\end{bmatrix}$

Scalar multiplication multiplies **every** entry by the scalar:
$$3A=3\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 3&6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\times1&3\times2\\ 3\times3&3\times6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\ 9&18\end{bmatrix}$$

$$\therefore\ 3A=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\ 9&18\end{bmatrix}$$

**Note the distractor:** option (2) multiplies only the second column, which is not how scalar multiplication works. Also $\det(3A)=3^{2}\det A=9(6-6)=0$, consistent with $3A$ having proportional rows ($\dfrac{3}{9}=\dfrac{6}{18}$).

questions.question: If $A$ and $B$ are two square matrices, then $(A+B)^{T}=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $A^{T}+B^{T}$

Transpose is **additive**: for matrices $A,B$ of the same order,
$$(A+B)^{T}=A^{T}+B^{T}$$

**Why?** The $(i,j)$ entry of $A+B$ is $a_{ij}+b_{ij}$; transposing moves it to the $(j,i)$ position, where it is $a_{ji}+b_{ji}$ — which is precisely the $(j,i)$ entry of $A^{T}$ plus that of $B^{T}$.

**Contrast with the product:** $(AB)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}$ — the order *reverses* for products, but not for sums. That distinction is the usual trap in this question.

$$\therefore\ (A+B)^{T}=A^{T}+B^{T}$$

questions.question: If $\begin{bmatrix}x+3&2x\\ 6&y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}7&8\\ 6&3\end{bmatrix}$, then values of $x$ and $y$ are
questions.answer:
**(A)** $x=4,\ y=3$

Compare corresponding entries.

**From the $(1,1)$ entry:**
$$x+3=7\ \Rightarrow\ x=4$$

**Consistency check with the $(1,2)$ entry:**
$$2x=8\ \Rightarrow\ x=4\ ✓$$
(the same value — the problem is consistent)

**From the $(2,2)$ entry:**
$$y=3$$

The $(2,1)$ entry gives $6=6$, automatically true.
$$\therefore\ x=4,\qquad y=3$$

Had the $(1,2)$ equation given a different $x$, the matrix equality would have been impossible — so it is worth always checking *all* entries, not just the first one that yields an answer.

questions.question: $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\ x+y&y+z&z+x\\ z&x&y\end{vmatrix}=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $0$

**Step 1 — expand along the first row.** Write
$$\Delta=1\begin{vmatrix}y+z&z+x\\ x&y\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}x+y&z+x\\ z&y\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}x+y&y+z\\ z&x\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — the three $2\times2$ minors:**
- $\begin{vmatrix}y+z&z+x\\ x&y\end{vmatrix}=(y+z)y-(z+x)x=y^{2}+yz-xz-x^{2}$
- $\begin{vmatrix}x+y&z+x\\ z&y\end{vmatrix}=(x+y)y-(z+x)z=xy+y^{2}-z^{2}-xz$
- $\begin{vmatrix}x+y&y+z\\ z&x\end{vmatrix}=(x+y)x-(y+z)z=x^{2}+xy-yz-z^{2}$

**Step 3 — substitute:**
$$\Delta=\left(y^{2}+yz-xz-x^{2}\right)-\left(xy+y^{2}-z^{2}-xz\right)+\left(x^{2}+xy-yz-z^{2}\right)$$

Collect like terms:
$$y^{2}-y^{2}=0,\quad -x^{2}+x^{2}=0,\quad z^{2}-z^{2}=0,\quad yz-yz=0,\quad -xz+xz=0,\quad -xy+xy=0$$

Every term cancels, so
$$\Delta=0\quad\text{identically in }x,y,z$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\ x+y&y+z&z+x\\ z&x&y\end{vmatrix}=0$$

**Numerical check:** with $x=1$, $y=2$, $z=3$ the matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\ 3&5&4\\ 3&1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\Delta=1(10-4)-1(6-12)+1(3-15)=6+6-12=0$ ✓.

**Why it must vanish:** the column sums are $C_{1}+C_{2}+C_{3}=\left(3,\ 2(x+y+z),\ x+y+z\right)^{T}$, and the row sums are row 1: $3$, row 2: $2(x+y+z)$, row 3: $x+y+z$ — the same vector. A matrix whose column sums equal its row sums in this paired way is linearly dependent, so the determinant is identically zero.**Simplest rigorous route — direct expansion.** Expanding along the first row,
$$\Delta=1\begin{vmatrix}y+z&z+x\\ x&y\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}x+y&z+x\\ z&y\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}x+y&y+z\\ z&x\end{vmatrix}$$

First minor: $(y+z)y-(z+x)x=y^{2}+yz-xz-x^{2}$.

Second minor: $(x+y)y-(z+x)z=xy+y^{2}-z^{2}-xz$.

Third minor: $(x+y)x-(y+z)z=x^{2}+xy-yz-z^{2}$.

Therefore
$$\Delta=\left(y^{2}+yz-xz-x^{2}\right)-\left(xy+y^{2}-z^{2}-xz\right)+\left(x^{2}+xy-yz-z^{2}\right)$$

Collect: $y^{2}-y^{2}=0$; $-x^{2}+x^{2}=0$; $-z^{2}+z^{2}=0$; $yz-yz=0$; $-xz+xz=0$; $-xy+xy=0$. Every term cancels:
$$\Delta=0$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\ x+y&y+z&z+x\\ z&x&y\end{vmatrix}=0\quad\text{identically in }x,y,z$$

**Numerical spot check:** with $x=1$, $y=2$, $z=3$ the matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\ 3&5&4\\ 3&1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\Delta=1(10-4)-1(6-12)+1(3-15)=6+6-12=0$ ✓.

**Why it must vanish:** $C_{1}+C_{2}+C_{3}=\left(3,\ 2(x+y+z),\ x+y+z\right)^{T}$ while $2\times$ (row sums) gives the same vector, so the three columns are linearly dependent — hence the determinant is zero for every choice of $x,y,z$.

questions.question: $\begin{vmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\ -\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{vmatrix}=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $1$

Expand the $2\times2$ determinant as $ad-bc$:
$$\begin{vmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta\\ -\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{vmatrix}=\left(\cos\theta\right)\left(\cos\theta\right)-\left(\sin\theta\right)\left(-\sin\theta\right)$$
$$=\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$$

$$\therefore\ \text{determinant}=1\quad\text{for every }\theta$$

**Geometric meaning:** the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$ is a rotation, and this one is its transpose (a rotation through $-\theta$). Rotations preserve area, so the determinant — the area scale factor — must be $1$, independent of $\theta$ ✓.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tan x^{2}\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $2x\sec^{2}\left(x^{2}\right)$

The function is $\tan u$ with $u=x^{2}$ — the square is on $x$ only, not on the tangent. Apply the chain rule:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\tan u=\sec^{2}u\cdot\frac{du}{dx}$$

With $u=x^{2}$, $\dfrac{du}{dx}=2x$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan x^{2}\right)=\sec^{2}\left(x^{2}\right)\cdot2x=2x\sec^{2}\left(x^{2}\right)$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\left(\tan x^{2}\right)=2x\sec^{2}\left(x^{2}\right)$$

**Note the contrast with $\tan^{2}x$** (the square of the tangent), whose derivative is $2\tan x\sec^{2}x$ — no factor $2x$ appears there. Reading the notation carefully is the whole point of this question.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^{-1}x\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$

This is a standard derivative, valid for $-1<x<1$. It follows from implicit differentiation: let $y=\sin^{-1}x$, so $x=\sin y$ with $y\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Then
$$1=\cos y\frac{dy}{dx}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\cos y}$$

Since $y\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\cos y>0$, so $\cos y=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}y}=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$:
$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$$

**Option (2) is the derivative of $\cos^{-1}x$** and **option (3) is the derivative of $\tan^{-1}x$** — the classic confusions. Note also $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, whose derivative is $0$, consistent with the two derivatives being exact negatives.

questions.question: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\log\sec x\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\tan x$

Apply the chain rule with outer function $\log$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sec x\right)=\frac{1}{\sec x}\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sec x\right)$$

Now $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x$, so
$$=\frac{1}{\sec x}\cdot\sec x\tan x=\tan x$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d}{dx}\left(\log\sec x\right)=\tan x$$

**Equivalent view:** $\log\sec x=\log\dfrac{1}{\cos x}=-\log\cos x$, so the derivative is $-\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}=\tan x$ ✓ — same answer by a shorter route. Hence $\displaystyle\int\tan x\,dx=\log\left|\sec x\right|+C$.

questions.question: If $x=a\cos\theta$, $y=a\sin\theta$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.answer:
**(D)** none of these — the correct value is $-\cot\theta$

**Step 1 — differentiate each variable with respect to the parameter $\theta$:**
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta}=-a\sin\theta,\qquad \frac{dy}{d\theta}=a\cos\theta$$

**Step 2 — divide:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}=\frac{a\cos\theta}{-a\sin\theta}=-\cot\theta$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\cot\theta$$

**None of the printed options is $-\cot\theta$**, so the answer is 'none of these'.

**Checks.** The parametric curve is the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=a^{2}$; differentiating implicitly, $2x+2y\,y'=0$ gives $y'=-\dfrac xy=-\dfrac{a\cos\theta}{a\sin\theta}=-\cot\theta$ ✓. At $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ the point is $\left(\dfrac{a}{\sqrt2},\dfrac{a}{\sqrt2}\right)$ and the tangent has slope $-1$, matching $-\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=-1$ ✓.

questions.question: If $x^{m}y^{n}=(x+y)^{m+n}$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac yx$

**Step 1 — take logarithms of both sides:**
$$m\log x+n\log y=(m+n)\log(x+y)$$

**Step 2 — differentiate implicitly with respect to $x$:**
$$\frac{m}{x}+\frac{n}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{m+n}{x+y}\left(1+\frac{dy}{dx}\right)$$

**Step 3 — collect the $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ terms:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}\left[\frac ny-\frac{m+n}{x+y}\right]=\frac{m+n}{x+y}-\frac mx$$

Left bracket:
$$\frac ny-\frac{m+n}{x+y}=\frac{n(x+y)-y(m+n)}{y(x+y)}=\frac{nx-my}{y(x+y)}$$

Right side:
$$\frac{m+n}{x+y}-\frac mx=\frac{x(m+n)-m(x+y)}{x(x+y)}=\frac{nx-my}{x(x+y)}$$

**Step 4 — divide:** the common factor $\dfrac{nx-my}{x+y}$ cancels,
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\dfrac{nx-my}{x(x+y)}}{\dfrac{nx-my}{y(x+y)}}=\frac{y}{x}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac yx$$

**Sanity check:** take $n=-m$, say $m=1$, $n=-1$. The equation becomes $\dfrac xy=1$, i.e. $x=y$, and along that line $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1=\dfrac yx$ ✓. Take $m=n=1$: then $xy=(x+y)^{2}$, i.e. $x^{2}+xy+y^{2}=0$, which has no real solutions except $x=y=0$ — consistent with an identity whose slope formula is well defined only off the origin.

questions.question: The slope of the curve $y^{2}=x$ at the point $(1,1)$ is
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac12$

Differentiate implicitly with respect to $x$:
$$2y\frac{dy}{dx}=1\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2y}$$

At $(1,1)$, where $y=1$:
$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(1,1)}=\frac{1}{2(1)}=\frac12$$

$$\therefore\ \text{slope}=\frac12$$

**Alternative route:** writing the curve as $y=\sqrt x$ (upper branch through $(1,1)$) gives $y'=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$, which at $x=1$ is $\dfrac12$ ✓. The point $(1,1)$ is on the curve since $1^{2}=1$ ✓.

questions.question: The slope of the normal to the curve $y=2x^{2}+3\sin x$ at $x=0$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-\dfrac13$

**Step 1 — the tangent slope:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=4x+3\cos x$$

At $x=0$:
$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=0}=0+3(1)=3$$

**Step 2 — the normal is perpendicular to the tangent**, so its slope is the negative reciprocal:
$$m_{\text{normal}}=-\frac{1}{m_{\text{tangent}}}=-\frac13$$

$$\therefore\ \text{slope of the normal}=-\frac13$$

**Check of the perpendicularity:** $3\times\left(-\dfrac13\right)=-1$ ✓. The point of contact is $\left(0,\ 0+0\right)=(0,0)$, so the normal there is $y=-\dfrac x3$.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\sec^{2}x\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\tan x+c$

Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^{2}x$, the integral is immediate:
$$\int\sec^{2}x\,dx=\tan x+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\sec^{2}x\,dx=\tan x+c$$

**Verification:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tan x+c\right)=\sec^{2}x$ ✓. Note that options (3) and (4) fail immediately: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cot x=-\csc^{2}x$, not $\sec^{2}x$ (and no constant of integration is shown there).

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\frac{\sec^{2}x}{\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x}\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\tan x-x+c$

**Step 1 — simplify the integrand:**
$$\frac{\sec^{2}x}{\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x}=\frac{1/\cos^{2}x}{1/\sin^{2}x}=\frac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x}=\tan^{2}x$$

**Step 2 — use $\tan^{2}x=\sec^{2}x-1$:**
$$\int\tan^{2}x\,dx=\int\left(\sec^{2}x-1\right)dx=\tan x-x+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{\sec^{2}x}{\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x}\,dx=\tan x-x+c$$

**Check by differentiating:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\tan x-x\right)=\sec^{2}x-1=\tan^{2}x$ ✓ — exactly the simplified integrand. (Option (1) is the negative of the right answer, and option (3) has both signs flipped.)

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{9+x^{2}}=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac13\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac x3\right)+c$

Use the standard form
$$\int\frac{dx}{a^{2}+x^{2}}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa+c$$

Here $a^{2}=9$, so $a=3$:
$$\int\frac{dx}{9+x^{2}}=\frac13\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x3\right)+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{dx}{9+x^{2}}=\frac13\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x3\right)+c$$

**Derivation (substitution $x=3\tan\theta$, $dx=3\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta$):**
$$\int\frac{3\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta}{9+9\tan^{2}\theta}=\int\frac{3\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta}{9\sec^{2}\theta}=\frac13\int d\theta=\frac{\theta}{3}=\frac13\tan^{-1}\frac x3\ ✓$$

**Check by differentiating:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac13\tan^{-1}\dfrac x3\right]=\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+x^{2}/9}\cdot\dfrac13=\dfrac{1}{9+x^{2}}$ ✓.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac x4\right)+c$

Use the standard form
$$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}\frac xa+c$$

with $a^{2}=16$, i.e. $a=4$:
$$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac x4\right)+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac x4\right)+c$$

**The log options are distractor traps:** the logarithmic standard form is $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}\pm a^{2}}}=\log\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}\pm a^{2}}\right|$ — it applies to a **plus** sign (or a minus sign with $a^{2}$ subtracted from $x^{2}$, i.e. $\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}$), not to $\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$.

**Check by differentiating:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}\dfrac x4=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}/16}}\cdot\dfrac14=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}$ ✓.

questions.question: The radius of a circle is increasing at the rate of $0.3$ cm/sec. The rate of increase of its perimeter is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $0.6\pi$ cm/sec

Let $r$ be the radius and $P$ the perimeter (circumference) at time $t$:
$$P=2\pi r$$

**Given:** $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=0.3$ cm/sec.

Differentiate with respect to $t$:
$$\frac{dP}{dt}=2\pi\frac{dr}{dt}=2\pi(0.3)=0.6\pi$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dP}{dt}=0.6\pi\ \text{cm/sec}\approx1.885\ \text{cm/sec}$$

**Note the contrast with area:** $A=\pi r^{2}$ gives $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt}$, which depends on $r$ and so keeps growing; the perimeter grows at the *constant* rate $2\pi\dfrac{dr}{dt}$, independent of the current radius — a useful distinguishing feature.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}x^{2}\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\dfrac{b^{3}-a^{3}}{3}$

Integrate and apply the limits (upper limit minus lower limit):
$$\int_{a}^{b}x^{2}\,dx=\left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{a}^{b}=\frac{b^{3}}{3}-\frac{a^{3}}{3}=\frac{b^{3}-a^{3}}{3}$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{a}^{b}x^{2}\,dx=\frac{b^{3}-a^{3}}{3}$$

**Checks:** for $a=0$, $b=3$ this gives $\dfrac{27}{3}=9$, while the area under $y=x^{2}$ from $0$ to $3$ is indeed $9$ ✓. Option (2) has the order of the limits reversed (it would be the negative), and option (3) uses the antiderivative of $x^{3}$ instead of $x^{2}$.

questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\sqrt3}\frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac{\pi}{12}$

The antiderivative of $\dfrac{1}{1+x^{2}}$ is $\tan^{-1}x$:
$$\int_{1}^{\sqrt3}\frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}=\left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_{1}^{\sqrt3}=\tan^{-1}\sqrt3-\tan^{-1}1$$

Now $\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\tan^{-1}1=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{4\pi-3\pi}{12}=\frac{\pi}{12}$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{1}^{\sqrt3}\frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}=\frac{\pi}{12}=15^{\circ}$$

**Sanity check:** the integrand is positive and the interval has length $\sqrt3-1\approx0.732$; the integrand ranges from $\dfrac12$ (at $x=1$) to $\dfrac14$ (at $x=\sqrt3$), so the integral lies between $0.732\times\dfrac14\approx0.183$ and $0.732\times\dfrac12\approx0.366$. And $\dfrac{\pi}{12}\approx0.262$ ✓.

questions.topic: Definite Integral of an Odd Function
questions.question: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^{9}x\,dx=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $0$

**Step 1 — check the parity.** Put $f(x)=\sin^{9}x$. Since $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$,
$$f(-x)=\left(-\sin x\right)^{9}=-\sin^{9}x=-f(x)$$
so $f$ is an **odd** function.

**Step 2 — use the symmetric-interval rule:** for an odd continuous function on $[-a,a]$,
$$\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=0$$

The interval $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ is symmetric about $0$, so
$$\therefore\ \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sin^{9}x\,dx=0$$

**Intuition:** the negative lobe on $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right]$ is the exact mirror image (with opposite sign) of the positive lobe on $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so the two cancel. The same argument gives $0$ for every odd power $\sin^{1}x,\sin^{3}x,\ldots$ over this interval.

questions.question: The order of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2}+2\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3}+9y=0$ is
questions.answer:
**(A)** $2$

**Order** = the order of the highest derivative occurring in the equation. Reading the first term as $\left(\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2}$ (the printed '$\dfrac{dy}{dx^{2}}$' is the usual typographical slip for the second derivative, since the powers $2$ and $3$ would otherwise make no sense together),
$$\left(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{2}+2\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3}+9y=0$$

The derivatives present are $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ (order 2) and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ (order 1). The highest is order $2$:
$$\therefore\ \text{order}=2$$

**Degree** (for completeness) is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation is cleared of radicals: here $2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{order}=2,\qquad \text{degree}=2$$

**Note on the printed question:** options include '4', which is the *sum* $2+3$ of the exponents — a distractor for students who confuse order with the exponents.

questions.question: The integrating factor of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\sec^{2}x=\tan x\cdot\sec^{2}x$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $e^{\tan x}$

The equation is linear in $y$ with
$$P=\sec^{2}x,\qquad Q=\tan x\sec^{2}x$$

**The integrating factor:**
$$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{\int\sec^{2}x\,dx}=e^{\tan x}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{I.F.}=e^{\tan x}$$

**Does it work?** Multiplying through by $e^{\tan x}$, the left side becomes
$$e^{\tan x}\frac{dy}{dx}+e^{\tan x}\sec^{2}x\,y=\frac{d}{dx}\left(ye^{\tan x}\right)$$
which is exactly the required exact-derivative form ✓. The solution is then
$$ye^{\tan x}=\int e^{\tan x}\tan x\sec^{2}x\,dx=e^{\tan x}\left(\tan x-1\right)+C$$
(integrating by parts with $u=\tan x$, $dv=e^{\tan x}\sec^{2}x\,dx$), i.e. $y=\tan x-1+Ce^{-\tan x}$.

*Note on the printed question:* the booklet prints the equation as a second-order one, $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}+y\sec^{2}x=\tan x\sec^{2}x$. An integrating factor in the above sense exists only for a **first-order** linear equation, so the intended equation is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y\sec^{2}x=\tan x\sec^{2}x$ (a typo in the superscript). The printed answer $e^{\tan x}$ is correct for that equation.

questions.question: If $x\hat i+2\hat j=3\hat i-y\hat j$, then find $(x,y)$.
questions.answer:
**(A)** $3,\ -2$

Two vectors are equal exactly when their corresponding components are equal.

**Comparing the $\hat i$ components:**
$$x=3$$

**Comparing the $\hat j$ components:**
$$2=-y\ \Rightarrow\ y=-2$$

There are no $\hat k$ components on either side (both are $0$), so nothing more is required.
$$\therefore\ (x,y)=(3,-2)$$

**Check:** $3\hat i+2\hat j=3\hat i-(-2)\hat j=3\hat i+2\hat j$ ✓ — an identity. The trap is the sign of $y$: the minus sign in $-y\hat j$ makes $y$ negative, not the coefficient $-2$.

questions.question: The position vector of the point $(1,0,2)$ is
questions.answer:
**(A)** $\hat i+2\hat k$

The position vector of a point $P(x,y,z)$ is
$$\vec{OP}=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$$

For $(1,0,2)$:
$$\vec{OP}=1\hat i+0\hat j+2\hat k=\hat i+2\hat k$$

$$\therefore\ \vec{OP}=\hat i+2\hat k$$

**Note that the $\hat j$ term is absent** — a zero $y$-coordinate removes the middle component entirely, which is why option (4) (which keeps a $\hat j$) is wrong. Also $\left|\vec{OP}\right|=\sqrt{1+0+4}=\sqrt5$, a quick check on the magnitude.

questions.question: The scalar dot product of vectors $5\hat i+\hat j-3\hat k$ and $3\hat i-4\hat j+7\hat k$ is
questions.answer:
**(B)** $-10$

Multiply matching components and add:
$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(5)(3)+(1)(-4)+(-3)(7)$$
$$=15-4-21=-10$$

$$\therefore\ \vec a\cdot\vec b=-10$$

**Interpretation:** the dot product is negative, so the angle between the two vectors is obtuse. Indeed
$$\cos\theta=\frac{-10}{\sqrt{25+1+9}\cdot\sqrt{9+16+49}}=\frac{-10}{\sqrt{35}\cdot\sqrt{74}}\approx\frac{-10}{50.9}\approx-0.196$$
giving $\theta\approx101.3^{\circ}$ — obtuse, as expected ✓.

questions.question: $\hat i\times\hat j=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\hat k$

The standard unit vectors form a right-handed system, and
$$\hat i\times\hat j=\hat k,\qquad \hat j\times\hat k=\hat i,\qquad \hat k\times\hat i=\hat j$$

$$\therefore\ \hat i\times\hat j=\hat k$$

**Why right-handed?** By definition $\hat i\times\hat j$ is perpendicular to both $\hat i$ and $\hat j$, hence along $\pm\hat k$; the right-hand rule (curl fingers from $\hat i$ towards $\hat j$, thumb points along the positive $z$-axis) selects $+\hat k$.

**Related facts:** $\hat j\times\hat i=-\hat k$ (reversing the order flips the sign), $\hat i\times\hat i=\vec 0$ (parallel vectors), and $\left|\hat i\times\hat j\right|=1\cdot1\cdot\sin90^{\circ}=1$ ✓ — consistent with $\hat k$ being a unit vector.

questions.question: $(\vec a-\vec b)\times(\vec a+\vec b)=$
questions.answer:
**(A)** $2(\vec a\times\vec b)$

Expand by distributivity (the cross product is linear in each argument):
$$(\vec a-\vec b)\times(\vec a+\vec b)=\vec a\times\vec a+\vec a\times\vec b-\vec b\times\vec a-\vec b\times\vec b$$

Now use two facts:
$$\vec a\times\vec a=\vec 0,\qquad \vec b\times\vec b=\vec 0,\qquad \vec b\times\vec a=-\left(\vec a\times\vec b\right)$$

Substituting:
$$=\vec 0+\vec a\times\vec b+\left(\vec a\times\vec b\right)-\vec 0=2\left(\vec a\times\vec b\right)$$

$$\therefore\ (\vec a-\vec b)\times(\vec a+\vec b)=2\left(\vec a\times\vec b\right)$$

**Geometric check:** the vector $2\left(\vec a\times\vec b\right)$ has magnitude $2ab\sin\theta$; the parallelogram spanned by $\vec a-\vec b$ and $\vec a+\vec b$ has diagonals of those lengths, and its area is twice the area $ab\sin\theta$ of the parallelogram on $\vec a,\vec b$ ✓. Option (3) is the form of the corresponding **dot**-product identity: $(\vec a-\vec b)\cdot(\vec a+\vec b)=|\vec a|^{2}-|\vec b|^{2}$.

questions.question: $\vec a\cdot\vec a=$
questions.answer:
**(C)** $|\vec a|^{2}$

Put $\theta=0$ in $\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta$ with $\vec b=\vec a$:
$$\vec a\cdot\vec a=|\vec a||\vec a|\cos0=|\vec a|^{2}$$

$$\therefore\ \vec a\cdot\vec a=|\vec a|^{2}$$

**In components:** if $\vec a=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ then
$$\vec a\cdot\vec a=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=|\vec a|^{2}\ ✓$$

**Consequence worth remembering:** $\vec a\cdot\vec a=0$ only when $\vec a=\vec 0$, which is why the dot product is *positive definite* — the property that makes it an inner product. Option (2) would be correct only for a unit vector, i.e. when $|\vec a|=1$.

questions.question: The direction cosines of $z$-axis are
questions.answer:
**(D)** $(0,0,1)$

Direction cosines are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the positive $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes.

The $z$-axis makes:
- angle $90^{\circ}$ with the $x$-axis, so $l=\cos90^{\circ}=0$
- angle $90^{\circ}$ with the $y$-axis, so $m=\cos90^{\circ}=0$
- angle $0^{\circ}$ with the $z$-axis itself, so $n=\cos0^{\circ}=1$

$$\therefore\ (l,m,n)=(0,0,1)$$

**Checks:** $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=0+0+1=1$ ✓ as every triple of direction cosines must satisfy. Correspondingly the $x$-axis has direction cosines $(1,0,0)$ — option (2) — and the $y$-axis $(0,1,0)$, option (3).

questions.question: Find the equation of the line joining $(-2,4,2)$ and $(7,-2,5)$.
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac{x+2}{3}=\dfrac{y-4}{-2}=\dfrac{z-2}{1}$

**Step 1 — direction ratios** (second point minus first):
$$(7-(-2),\ -2-4,\ 5-2)=(9,-6,3)$$

Dividing by $3$ gives the simpler proportional triple $(3,-2,1)$ — any non-zero multiple gives the same line.

**Step 2 — use one point**, say $(-2,4,2)$, with the symmetric form
$$\frac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\frac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\frac{z-z_{1}}{c}$$
$$\therefore\ \frac{x+2}{3}=\frac{y-4}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$$

**Check that the second point lies on it:** at $(7,-2,5)$,
$$\frac{7+2}{3}=3,\qquad \frac{-2-4}{-2}=3,\qquad \frac{5-2}{1}=3$$
all equal ✓. Options (1) and (2) would be lines through the **origin** with the direction or position numbers of these points — a common trap.

questions.question: Line $\dfrac{x-5}{3}=\dfrac{y+4}{7}=\dfrac{z-6}{2}$ passes through the point
questions.answer:
**(A)** $(5,-4,6)$

The symmetric form $\dfrac{x-x_{1}}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_{1}}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_{1}}{c}$ passes through $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})$.

Comparing, $x-x_{1}=x-5$ gives $x_{1}=5$; $y-y_{1}=y+4=y-(-4)$ gives $y_{1}=-4$; $z-z_{1}=z-6$ gives $z_{1}=6$:
$$\therefore\ \text{the line passes through }(5,-4,6)$$

**Verification by substitution:** at $(5,-4,6)$ all three fractions become $\dfrac03=\dfrac07=\dfrac02=0$ ✓ — the point corresponds to the parameter value $0$.

**Option (2) is the sign trap:** $(5,4,-6)$ would give $\dfrac03$, $\dfrac87$, $\dfrac{-12}{2}$ — not equal, so it is not on the line.

questions.question: The direction cosines of the normal to the plane $2x-3y-6z-3=0$ are
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\dfrac27,-\dfrac37,-\dfrac67$

**Step 1 — read off the normal.** For $ax+by+cz+d=0$ the normal is $(a,b,c)$; here
$$\vec n=(2,-3,-6)$$

**Step 2 — divide by its magnitude:**
$$|\vec n|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-3)^{2}+(-6)^{2}}=\sqrt{4+9+36}=\sqrt{49}=7$$

$$\therefore\ \text{direction cosines}=\left(\frac{2}{7},\ -\frac{3}{7},\ -\frac{6}{7}\right)$$

**Check:** $\dfrac{4+9+36}{49}=1$ ✓. Note the signs must match the coefficients of the plane exactly — option (2) flips the sign of the $y$ component and option (1) reverses the first two signs, so only (3) is the correct triple (both $\pm$ triples describe the same line of action, but the direction cosines *of the given normal* are the ones with the coefficients' own signs).

questions.topic: Distance from a Point to a Plane
questions.question: Find the perpendicular distance of the plane $2x+y-2z+1=0$ from the point $(0,-1,3)$.
questions.answer:
**(C)** $2$

The distance from $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})$ to $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is
$$d=\frac{\left|ax_{1}+by_{1}+cz_{1}+d\right|}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}$$

Here $a=2$, $b=1$, $c=-2$, $d=1$ and $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})=(0,-1,3)$.

**Numerator:**
$$\left|2(0)+1(-1)-2(3)+1\right|=\left|-1-6+1\right|=\left|-6\right|=6$$

**Denominator:**
$$\sqrt{4+1+4}=\sqrt9=3$$

$$d=\frac63=2$$

$$\therefore\ \text{perpendicular distance}=2\ \text{units}$$

**Check the point's side:** the signed value is $\dfrac{-6}{3}=-2<0$, so the point lies on the negative side of the plane — the distance itself is the magnitude, $2$.

questions.question: If $P(A)=\dfrac38$, $P(B)=\dfrac12$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac14$, then $P\left(\dfrac AB\right)=$
questions.answer:
**(B)** $\dfrac12$

By the definition of conditional probability,
$$P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$$

Substitute:
$$P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac14\cdot\frac21=\frac12$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac12$$

**Cross-check with the other conditional:** $P\left(\dfrac BA\right)=\dfrac{1/4}{3/8}=\dfrac{2}{3}$, and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac38+\dfrac12-\dfrac14=\dfrac{5}{8}$. Consistency: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B/A)=\dfrac38\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac14$ ✓.

questions.question: If $P(A)=\dfrac38$, $P(B)=\dfrac13$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac14$, then $P(A\cup B)=$
questions.answer:
**(D)** none of these — the value is $\dfrac{11}{24}$

By the addition theorem,
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$$

Substitute, using the common denominator $24$:
$$=\frac38+\frac13-\frac14=\frac{9}{24}+\frac{8}{24}-\frac{6}{24}=\frac{11}{24}$$

$$\therefore\ P(A\cup B)=\frac{11}{24}\approx0.458$$

**None of the printed options equals $\dfrac{11}{24}$** — $\dfrac23=\dfrac{16}{24}$, $\dfrac13=\dfrac{8}{24}$ and $\dfrac12=\dfrac{12}{24}$ all differ — so the answer is 'none of these'.

**Sanity check:** $P(A\cup B)\le1$ ✓; and it must exceed each of $P(A)=\dfrac{9}{24}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{8}{24}$, which $\dfrac{11}{24}$ does ✓.

questions.question: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ and $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ are defined by $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=x^{2}$, then find $f\circ g(x)$.
questions.answer:
By definition, $f\circ g(x)=f\left(g(x)\right)$ — apply $g$ first, then $f$:
$$f\circ g(x)=f\left(x^{2}\right)=\sqrt{x^{2}}$$

Now $\sqrt{x^{2}}$ is **not** $x$ for all real $x$; it is the modulus:
$$\sqrt{x^{2}}=|x|=\begin{cases}x,&x\ge0\\ -x,&x<0\end{cases}$$

$$\therefore\ f\circ g(x)=|x|,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}$$

**Checks:** at $x=3$, $f(g(3))=f(9)=3=|3|$ ✓; at $x=-3$, $f(g(-3))=f(9)=3=|-3|$ ✓ (and not $-3$).

**Contrast:** $g\circ f(x)=g\left(\sqrt x\right)=\left(\sqrt x\right)^{2}=x$, but only for $x\ge0$, since $\sqrt x$ requires $x\ge0$. So $f\circ g=|x|$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$ while $g\circ f=x$ merely on $[0,\infty)$ — composition is not commutative.

questions.question: Prove that $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{11}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7}{24}\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right)$.
questions.answer:
Use the addition formula
$$\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\frac{x+y}{1-xy}\qquad(xy<1)$$

with $x=\dfrac{2}{11}$, $y=\dfrac{7}{24}$. Here $xy=\dfrac{14}{264}=\dfrac{7}{132}<1$, so no adjustment by $\pi$ is needed.

**Numerator:**
$$x+y=\frac{2}{11}+\frac{7}{24}=\frac{48+77}{264}=\frac{125}{264}$$

**Denominator:**
$$1-xy=1-\frac{14}{264}=\frac{250}{264}$$

**Divide:**
$$\frac{x+y}{1-xy}=\frac{125/264}{250/264}=\frac{125}{250}=\frac12$$

$$\therefore\ \tan^{-1}\frac{2}{11}+\tan^{-1}\frac{7}{24}=\tan^{-1}\frac12\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Numerical check:** $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{11}\approx10.30^{\circ}$ and $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{7}{24}\approx16.26^{\circ}$, sum $\approx26.57^{\circ}$; and $\tan^{-1}\dfrac12\approx26.57^{\circ}$ ✓.

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3&5\\ 4&6&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}2&-4\\ 1&-3\\ 4&0\end{bmatrix}$, then find $AB$.
questions.answer:
$A$ is $2\times3$ and $B$ is $3\times2$, so $AB$ is $2\times2$. Each entry is a row of $A$ dotted with a column of $B$.

**Row 1 of $A$ = $(2,3,5)$:**

$$(AB)_{11}=2(2)+3(1)+5(4)=4+3+20=27$$
$$(AB)_{12}=2(-4)+3(-3)+5(0)=-8-9+0=-17$$

**Row 2 of $A$ = $(4,6,2)$:**

$$(AB)_{21}=4(2)+6(1)+2(4)=8+6+8=22$$
$$(AB)_{22}=4(-4)+6(-3)+2(0)=-16-18+0=-34$$

$$\therefore\ AB=\begin{bmatrix}27&-17\\ 22&-34\end{bmatrix}$$

**Note:** $BA$ would be $3\times3$ — a different order of matrix entirely — so it cannot be compared with $AB$; matrix multiplication is not commutative even in size.

questions.question: If $y=x^{\sin x}$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.answer:
The variable appears in **both** the base and the exponent, so take logarithms.

**Step 1 — take $\log$:**
$$\log y=\sin x\cdot\log x$$

**Step 2 — differentiate both sides** (product rule on the right):
$$\frac1y\frac{dy}{dx}=\sin x\cdot\frac{1}{x}+\cos x\cdot\log x$$

**Step 3 — multiply by $y$ and restore $y=x^{\sin x}$:**
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{\sin x}\left[\frac{\sin x}{x}+\cos x\log x\right]$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dy}{dx}=x^{\sin x}\left[\frac{\sin x}{x}+\cos x\,\log x\right]$$

**Validity:** the derivation needs $x>0$, so that both $\log x$ and the real power $x^{\sin x}=e^{\sin x\log x}$ are defined.

**Special-value check:** at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ we have $y=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^{1}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $y'=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{\pi/2}+0\cdot\log\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2}{\pi}=1$; direct differentiation of $y=x$ near $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (where $\sin x\approx1$) also suggests slope $\approx1$ ✓.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{\cos x}{\sqrt{1+\sin x}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — substitute** $t=1+\sin x$, so that $dt=\cos x\,dx$ — exactly the numerator:
$$\int\frac{\cos x\,dx}{\sqrt{1+\sin x}}=\int\frac{dt}{\sqrt t}=\int t^{-1/2}dt$$

**Step 2 — integrate the power:**
$$\int t^{-1/2}dt=\frac{t^{1/2}}{1/2}=2\sqrt t+C$$

**Step 3 — back-substitute:**
$$\therefore\ \int\frac{\cos x}{\sqrt{1+\sin x}}\,dx=2\sqrt{1+\sin x}+C$$

**Check by differentiating:**
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[2\left(1+\sin x\right)^{1/2}\right]=2\cdot\frac12\left(1+\sin x\right)^{-1/2}\cdot\cos x=\frac{\cos x}{\sqrt{1+\sin x}}\ ✓$$

questions.question: Solve the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1+x^{2}}{1+y^{2}}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — separate the variables** (multiply across by $1+y^{2}$ and by $dx$):
$$\left(1+y^{2}\right)dy=\left(1+x^{2}\right)dx$$

**Step 2 — integrate both sides:**
$$\int\left(1+y^{2}\right)dy=\int\left(1+x^{2}\right)dx$$

$$y+\frac{y^{3}}{3}=x+\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C$$

$$\therefore\ 3y+y^{3}=3x+x^{3}+K\qquad(K=3C)$$

which is the general solution in implicit form.

**Check by implicit differentiation:** differentiate $y+\dfrac{y^{3}}{3}=x+\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}+C$ with respect to $x$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}\left(1+y^{2}\right)=1+x^{2}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1+x^{2}}{1+y^{2}}\ ✓$$

**Note:** the right side is positive for all $x$, so $y$ is an increasing function of $x$ everywhere — consistent with the displayed solution family.

questions.question: Compute $P\left(\dfrac AB\right)$ if $P(B)=0.5$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.32$.
questions.answer:
By definition,
$$P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$$

Substitute the given values:
$$P\left(\frac AB\right)=\frac{0.32}{0.5}=\frac{32}{50}=0.64$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac AB\right)=0.64$$

**Interpretation:** knowing that $B$ has occurred raises the chance of $A$ from its unconditional $P(A)$ (which is not given but must satisfy $P(A)\ge P(A\cap B)=0.32$); the conditional value $0.64$ is exactly the fraction of $B$'s probability that is shared with $A$.

**Consistency:** $P(A\cap B)\le P(B)$ requires $0.32\le0.5$ ✓, so the data are admissible.

questions.question: Prove that $\begin{vmatrix}x+\lambda&x&x\\ x&x+\lambda&x\\ x&x&x+\lambda\end{vmatrix}=(3x+\lambda)\lambda^{2}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — add the other two columns to the first:** $C_{1}\to C_{1}+C_{2}+C_{3}$. Each entry of the new first column becomes
$$(x+\lambda)+x+x=3x+\lambda$$

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}3x+\lambda&x&x\\ 3x+\lambda&x+\lambda&x\\ 3x+\lambda&x&x+\lambda\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — take the common factor out of the first column:**
$$\Delta=\left(3x+\lambda\right)\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x\\ 1&x+\lambda&x\\ 1&x&x+\lambda\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — clear the first column** with $R_{2}\to R_{2}-R_{1}$ and $R_{3}\to R_{3}-R_{1}$:
$$R_{2}=\left(0,\ \lambda,\ 0\right),\qquad R_{3}=\left(0,\ 0,\ \lambda\right)$$

$$\Delta=\left(3x+\lambda\right)\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x\\ 0&\lambda&0\\ 0&0&\lambda\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 4 — the remaining determinant is upper triangular**, so it equals the product of its diagonal entries:
$$\Delta=\left(3x+\lambda\right)\cdot1\cdot\lambda\cdot\lambda=\left(3x+\lambda\right)\lambda^{2}$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}x+\lambda&x&x\\ x&x+\lambda&x\\ x&x&x+\lambda\end{vmatrix}=\left(3x+\lambda\right)\lambda^{2}\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Numerical check:** with $x=1$, $\lambda=2$ the matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}3&1&1\\ 1&3&1\\ 1&1&3\end{bmatrix}$, whose determinant is $3(9-1)-1(3-1)+1(1-3)=24-2-2=20$; and $(3\cdot1+2)\cdot2^{2}=5\cdot4=20$ ✓.

questions.question: If $f(x)=2x+5$ when $x\le2$ and $f(x)=2x-5$ when $x>2$, then test the continuity of $f(x)$ at $x=2$.
questions.answer:
For continuity at $x=2$ we need
$$\lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=f(2)=\lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)$$

**Left-hand limit** (branch valid for $x\le2$):
$$\lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2}\left(2x+5\right)=4+5=9$$

**Value at the point:** $f(2)=2(2)+5=9$ — so the left limit and value agree.

**Right-hand limit** (branch valid for $x>2$):
$$\lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2}\left(2x-5\right)=4-5=-1$$

**Compare:**
$$\lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=9\neq-1=\lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)$$

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is \textbf{not continuous} at }x=2$$

The graph has a **jump discontinuity** there: as $x$ approaches $2$ from below the values tend to $9$, and from above to $-1$, so the jump has size $9-(-1)=10$. The function is continuous everywhere else (each branch is a polynomial, and the split point $2$ is the only place the formula changes).

questions.question: Find the interval in which the function $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5$ is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — differentiate:**
$$f'(x)=2x+2=2(x+1)$$

**Step 2 — the critical point** from $f'(x)=0$:
$$x=-1$$

**Step 3 — sign of $f'(x)=2(x+1)$:**

| Interval | Sign of $x+1$ | $f'(x)$ | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(-\infty,-1)$ | $-$ | $-$ | decreasing |
| $(-1,\infty)$ | $+$ | $+$ | increasing |

$$\therefore\ f\ \text{is strictly decreasing on }(-\infty,-1)\ \text{and strictly increasing on }(-1,\infty)$$

**Check with the geometry:** $f(x)=x^{2}+2x-5=(x+1)^{2}-6$ is an upward parabola with vertex at $(-1,-6)$ — it falls to the vertex and then rises ✓. The minimum value is $f(-1)=1-2-5=-6$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{2x+1}{x^{2}+4x-3}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the denominator plus a constant.** The derivative of the denominator is $2x+4$, so write
$$2x+1=A(2x+4)+B$$

Comparing coefficients:
$$2A=2\ \Rightarrow\ A=1$$
$$4A+B=1\ \Rightarrow\ B=1-4=-3$$

$$\therefore\ 2x+1=\left(2x+4\right)-3$$

**Step 2 — split the integral:**
$$I=\int\frac{2x+4}{x^{2}+4x-3}\,dx-3\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+4x-3}$$

**Step 3 — the first piece** is a log (substitute $t=x^{2}+4x-3$, $dt=(2x+4)dx$):
$$\int\frac{2x+4}{x^{2}+4x-3}\,dx=\log\left|x^{2}+4x-3\right|$$

**Step 4 — the second piece.** Complete the square:
$$x^{2}+4x-3=(x+2)^{2}-7=(x+2)^{2}-\left(\sqrt7\right)^{2}$$

Use $\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{u^{2}-a^{2}}=\frac{1}{2a}\log\left|\frac{u-a}{u+a}\right|$ with $u=x+2$, $a=\sqrt7$:
$$\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+4x-3}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt7}\log\left|\frac{x+2-\sqrt7}{x+2+\sqrt7}\right|$$

**Step 5 — combine:**
$$\therefore\ I=\log\left|x^{2}+4x-3\right|-\frac{3}{2\sqrt7}\log\left|\frac{x+2-\sqrt7}{x+2+\sqrt7}\right|+C$$

**Check by differentiating:** the first term gives $\dfrac{2x+4}{x^{2}+4x-3}$; the second gives $-3\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt7}\left[\dfrac{1}{x+2-\sqrt7}-\dfrac{1}{x+2+\sqrt7}\right]=-3\cdot\dfrac{2\sqrt7}{2\sqrt7\left(x^{2}+4x-3\right)}=\dfrac{-3}{x^{2}+4x-3}$. Together: $\dfrac{2x+4-3}{x^{2}+4x-3}=\dfrac{2x+1}{x^{2}+4x-3}$ ✓.

**Note:** $x^{2}+4x-3$ has real roots $-2\pm\sqrt7$, so its sign is not fixed and the modulus signs are necessary.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let
$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}\,dx\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**Step 1 — apply $x\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}-x$**, using $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(a-x)dx$. Under this substitution $\tan x\to\cot x$ and $\cot x\to\tan x$:
$$I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\cot x}}{\sqrt{\cot x}+\sqrt{\tan x}}\,dx\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Step 2 — add (1) and (2).** The denominators are identical; the numerators add to exactly the denominator:
$$2I=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}\,dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}1\,dx$$

**Step 3 — evaluate:**
$$2I=\left[x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}=\frac{\pi}{2}$$
$$I=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\sqrt{\tan x}+\sqrt{\cot x}}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

**Remark:** the same trick works with any power — $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{f(\tan x)}{f(\tan x)+f(\cot x)}dx=\frac{\pi}{4}$ for every positive function $f$, since the substitution merely swaps the two halves of the integrand.

questions.topic: Area Between a Parabola and a Line
questions.question: Find the area of a region bounded by the curve $y^{2}=4x$ and the straight line $x=3$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — a sketch.** The curve $y^{2}=4x$ is a parabola opening to the right with vertex at the origin; the line $x=3$ cuts it at the points where $y^{2}=12$, i.e. $y=\pm2\sqrt3$. The enclosed region is the 'cap' between the parabola's two branches and the vertical line.

**Step 2 — integrate along $y$** (easier here, since the right and left boundaries are single functions of $y$). For a given $y\in\left[-2\sqrt3,\,2\sqrt3\right]$ the region runs from the parabola $x=\dfrac{y^{2}}{4}$ to the line $x=3$:
$$A=\int_{-2\sqrt3}^{2\sqrt3}\left(3-\frac{y^{2}}{4}\right)dy$$

**Step 3 — exploit the symmetry in $y$** (the integrand is even):
$$A=2\int_{0}^{2\sqrt3}\left(3-\frac{y^{2}}{4}\right)dy=2\left[3y-\frac{y^{3}}{12}\right]_{0}^{2\sqrt3}$$

At $y=2\sqrt3$: $3(2\sqrt3)=6\sqrt3$ and $\dfrac{\left(2\sqrt3\right)^{3}}{12}=\dfrac{8\cdot3\sqrt3}{12}=2\sqrt3$, so
$$A=2\left(6\sqrt3-2\sqrt3\right)=2\left(4\sqrt3\right)=8\sqrt3$$

$$\therefore\ A=8\sqrt3\ \text{sq. units}\approx13.86$$

**Cross-check by integrating along $x$:** the region is symmetric about the $x$-axis, so
$$A=2\int_{0}^{3}2\sqrt x\,dx=4\left[\frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_{0}^{3}=\frac{8}{3}\cdot3\sqrt3=8\sqrt3\ ✓$$
— the same value, confirming the setup.

questions.question: Find the angle between the following pair of lines: $\vec r=\left(3\hat i+2\hat j-4\hat k\right)+\lambda\left(\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=\left(5\hat i-2\hat j+\hat k\right)+t\left(3\hat i+2\hat j+6\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — read the direction vectors.**
$$\vec b_{1}=\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{2}=3\hat i+2\hat j+6\hat k$$

**Step 2 — the angle formula**
$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}}{\left|\vec b_{1}\right|\left|\vec b_{2}\right|}$$

**Numerator:**
$$\vec b_{1}\cdot\vec b_{2}=(1)(3)+(2)(2)+(2)(6)=3+4+12=19$$

**Magnitudes:**
$$\left|\vec b_{1}\right|=\sqrt{1+4+4}=\sqrt9=3,\qquad \left|\vec b_{2}\right|=\sqrt{9+4+36}=\sqrt{49}=7$$

**Step 3 — compute:**
$$\cos\theta=\frac{19}{3\times7}=\frac{19}{21}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{19}{21}\right)\approx25.2^{\circ}$$

Since $\cos\theta>0$ the angle is acute, which is the standard convention for the angle between two lines.

**Check:** $\dfrac{19}{21}\approx0.905$, and $\cos^{-1}0.905\approx25.2^{\circ}$; both direction vectors point 'mostly along $x$ and $z$' so a fairly small angle is plausible ✓.

questions.topic: System of Equations by Matrix Method
questions.question: Solve the system of the linear equations, using matrix method: $3x-y+z=5$, $2x-2y+3z=7$, $x+y-z=-1$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — write as $AX=B$:**
$$\begin{bmatrix}3&-1&1\\ 2&-2&3\\ 1&1&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5\\ 7\\ -1\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — the determinant:**
$$|A|=3\begin{vmatrix}-2&3\\ 1&-1\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\ 1&-1\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}2&-2\\ 1&1\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=3(2-3)+1(-2-3)+1(2+2)$$
$$=-3-5+4=-4$$

Since $|A|=-4\neq0$, $A^{-1}$ exists and $X=A^{-1}B$ is unique.

**Step 3 — the cofactors:**
$$C_{11}=+\left(2-3\right)=-1\qquad C_{12}=-\left(-2-3\right)=5\qquad C_{13}=+\left(2+2\right)=4$$
$$C_{21}=-\left(1-1\right)=0\qquad C_{22}=+\left(-3-1\right)=-4\qquad C_{23}=-\left(3+1\right)=-4$$
$$C_{31}=+\left(-3+2\right)=-1\qquad C_{32}=-\left(9-2\right)=-7\qquad C_{33}=+\left(-6+2\right)=-4$$

**Step 4 — the adjoint** (cofactor matrix transposed):
$$\text{adj}\,A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&-1\\ 5&-4&-7\\ 4&-4&-4\end{bmatrix}$$

$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&-1\\ 5&-4&-7\\ 4&-4&-4\end{bmatrix}=\frac14\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\ -5&4&7\\ -4&4&4\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 5 — multiply by $B$:**
$$x=\frac14\left[(1)(5)+0(7)+(1)(-1)\right]=\frac{5-1}{4}=1$$
$$y=\frac14\left[(-5)(5)+(4)(7)+(7)(-1)\right]=\frac{-25+28-7}{4}=\frac{-4}{4}=-1$$
$$z=\frac14\left[(-4)(5)+(4)(7)+(4)(-1)\right]=\frac{-20+28-4}{4}=\frac44=1$$

$$\therefore\ x=1,\quad y=-1,\quad z=1$$

**Check in the original equations:** $3(1)-(-1)+1=5$ ✓; $2(1)-2(-1)+3(1)=2+2+3=7$ ✓; $1+(-1)-1=-1$ ✓.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of the given function: $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x+5$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — first derivative:**
$$f'(x)=3x^{2}-12x+9=3\left(x^{2}-4x+3\right)=3(x-1)(x-3)$$

**Step 2 — second derivative:**
$$f''(x)=6x-12$$

**Step 3 — critical points** from $f'(x)=0$:
$$x=1,\qquad x=3$$

**Step 4 — test each.**

*At $x=1$:*
$$f''(1)=6-12=-6<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local maximum}$$
$$f(1)=1-6+9+5=9$$

*At $x=3$:*
$$f''(3)=18-12=6>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum}$$
$$f(3)=27-54+27+5=5$$

**Step 5 — conclusion.**

| $x$ | $f''(x)$ | Nature | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| $1$ | $-6$ | local maximum | $9$ |
| $3$ | $6$ | local minimum | $5$ |

$$\therefore\ \text{maximum value}=9\ \text{at }x=1;\qquad \text{minimum value}=5\ \text{at }x=3$$

**These are local (relative) extrema only** — because $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+9x+5\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$ and $\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$, the function has no absolute maximum or minimum on $\mathbb{R}$. A quick check of the shape: $f$ increases up to $x=1$, falls to $x=3$, then rises again — exactly the pattern found.

questions.question: Find the shortest distance between the lines $\vec r=\left(\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k\right)+t\left(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=\left(2\hat i+4\hat j+5\hat k\right)+\lambda\left(3\hat i+4\hat j+5\hat k\right)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — read off the data:**
$$\vec a_{1}=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{1}=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k$$
$$\vec a_{2}=2\hat i+4\hat j+5\hat k,\qquad \vec b_{2}=3\hat i+4\hat j+5\hat k$$

The lines are (skew) in general position, so
$$d=\frac{\left|\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right)\right|}{\left|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right|}$$

**Step 2 — a vector joining the two given points:**
$$\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}=\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$$

**Step 3 — the cross product of the directions:**
$$\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 2&3&4\\ 3&4&5\end{vmatrix}$$
$$=\hat i\left[(3)(5)-(4)(4)\right]-\hat j\left[(2)(5)-(4)(3)\right]+\hat k\left[(2)(4)-(3)(3)\right]$$
$$=\hat i(15-16)-\hat j(10-12)+\hat k(8-9)$$
$$=-\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k$$

$${\left|\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right|}=\sqrt{1+4+1}=\sqrt6$$

**Step 4 — the scalar triple product:**
$$\left(\vec a_{2}-\vec a_{1}\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_{1}\times\vec b_{2}\right)=(1)(-1)+(2)(2)+(2)(-1)=-1+4-2=1$$

**Step 5 — the distance:**
$$d=\frac{|1|}{\sqrt6}=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}{6}$$

$$\therefore\ d=\frac{\sqrt6}{6}\approx0.408\ \text{units}$$

**Since $d\neq0$**, the two lines do not intersect — they are genuinely skew, which is consistent with $\vec b_{1}$ and $\vec b_{2}$ being non-parallel.

questions.question: Solve the LPP graphically: Maximise $Z=4x+y$ subject to constraints $x+y\le5$, $3x+y\le9$, $x\ge0$, $y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the boundary lines.**

**Line 1:** $x+y=5$; intercepts $(5,0)$ and $(0,5)$. The origin gives $0\le5$ ✓, so the feasible side contains the origin.

**Line 2:** $3x+y=9$; intercepts $(3,0)$ and $(0,9)$. The origin gives $0\le9$ ✓, again the side containing the origin.

**Step 2 — the corner points** (vertices of the feasible polygon in the first quadrant).

- $O(0,0)$.
- $A(3,0)$ — where line 2 meets the $x$-axis (the point $(5,0)$ of line 1 is outside $3x+y\le9$ since $15>9$).
- $B(0,5)$ — where line 1 meets the $y$-axis (the point $(0,9)$ of line 2 is outside $x+y\le5$).
- $C$ — where the two lines cross: solve
$$x+y=5,\qquad 3x+y=9$$
Subtract the first from the second: $2x=4\Rightarrow x=2$; then $y=5-2=3$:
$$C(2,3)$$

**Step 3 — evaluate $Z=4x+y$ at every corner.**

| Vertex | $Z=4x+y$ |
|---|---|
| $O(0,0)$ | $0$ |
| $A(3,0)$ | $12$ |
| $C(2,3)$ | $8+3=11$ |
| $B(0,5)$ | $5$ |

**Step 4 — conclusion.** The largest value is $12$, at $A(3,0)$:
$$\therefore\ Z_{\max}=12\quad\text{at}\quad x=3,\ y=0$$

**Check the feasibility of $A(3,0)$:** $3+0=3\le5$ ✓ and $9+0=9\le9$ ✓ (the second constraint is tight there, which is what makes $A$ a corner). Since $x\le3$ forced by the tight constraint and $Z$ increases fastest in the $x$ direction (coefficient $4$ versus $1$), the maximum indeed sits at $A$.

questions.question: A man is known to speak truth $3$ times out of $5$ times. He throws a die and reports that it is one (1) on the die. Find the probability that it is actually one (1) on the die.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — set up the events.**
- $E_{1}$: the die actually shows $1$, with $P\left(E_{1}\right)=\dfrac16$
- $E_{2}$: the die shows something other than $1$, with $P\left(E_{2}\right)=\dfrac56$
- $A$: the man **reports** that it is $1$

**Step 2 — the conditional probabilities.** The man speaks the truth with probability $\dfrac35$ and lies with probability $\dfrac25$.

If the die really is $1$ (truth needed):
$$P\left(\frac{A}{E_{1}}\right)=\frac35$$

If the die is not $1$, he must **lie** in order to say '$1$'. A liar picks one of the **five** wrong faces, so
$$P\left(\frac{A}{E_{2}}\right)=\frac25\times\frac15=\frac{2}{25}$$

**Step 3 — Bayes' theorem:**
$$P\left(\frac{E_{1}}{A}\right)=\frac{P\left(E_{1}\right)P\left(\frac{A}{E_{1}}\right)}{P\left(E_{1}\right)P\left(\frac{A}{E_{1}}\right)+P\left(E_{2}\right)P\left(\frac{A}{E_{2}}\right)}$$

$$=\frac{\dfrac16\cdot\dfrac35}{\dfrac16\cdot\dfrac35+\dfrac56\cdot\dfrac{2}{25}}=\frac{\dfrac{3}{30}}{\dfrac{3}{30}+\dfrac{10}{150}}$$

Put over the common denominator $150$: $\dfrac{3}{30}=\dfrac{15}{150}$ and $\dfrac{10}{150}=\dfrac{10}{150}$:
$$=\frac{15/150}{25/150}=\frac{15}{25}=\frac35$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac{E_{1}}{A}\right)=\frac35=0.6$$

**Interpretation:** the prior was only $\dfrac16\approx0.167$, but his testimony is fairly reliable ($\dfrac35$), so the posterior jumps to $\dfrac35$. It is not $1$ because he may be lying and happen to name '$1$' anyway — that possibility is exactly the second term in the denominator.

**Limiting cases as a check.** If the man were perfectly truthful ($p=1$), only the first term in the denominator would survive and the posterior would be $1$; if he always lied ($p=0$), the posterior would be $0$. For $p=\dfrac35$ the value $\dfrac35$ lies between these extremes, as it must — the posterior can never exceed the reliability of the witness.
